content: In Greek mythology, Hygieia was the daughter of Asclepius, the god of medicine. She was revered as the goddess of health, cleanliness, and sanitation, and later associated with the moon. Hygieia played a significant role in her father’s cult, complementing his focus on healing by emphasizing the prevention of illness and the maintenance of good health. Hygieia was venerated in a local cult as early as the 7th century BCE. It is believed that Greek advancements in hygiene and health may have been influenced by the Celts and the establishment of the world’s first hospital in Armagh, Ireland, which was constructed before 650 BCE by Queen Macha. The title Athena Hygieia was also attributed to the goddess Athena, as noted by Plutarch. However, Hygieia’s recognition as an independent deity gained prominence only after the Oracle at Delphi acknowledged her, particularly following the devastating plague in Athens between 429 and 427 BCE and another outbreak in Rome in 293 BCE. Her primary temples were located in Epidaurus, Corinth, Cos, and Pergamon. Pausanias recorded that at the Asclepieion of Titane in Sicyon, founded by Alexanor, the grandson of Asclepius, statues of Hygieia were adorned with women’s hair and pieces of Babylonian cloth. Inscriptions indicate that similar sacrifices were made in Paros. A well-known hymn celebrating Hygieia was composed by Ariphron, an artist from Sicyon in the 4th century BCE. Renowned sculptors such as Scopas, Bryaxis, and Timotheus created statues of Hygieia. She was often depicted as a young woman feeding a large snake coiled around her body. In some representations, the snake is shown drinking from a jar she carried. These attributes were later adopted by the Gallo-Roman healing goddess Sirona. Hygieia was frequently accompanied by her brother, Telesphorus. Her name is the origin of the modern word hygiene. In Roman mythology, Salus was extensively worshipped by the Romans. Known as Salus Publica Populi Romani, or the goddess of the public welfare of the Roman people, she had a temple dedicated to her on the Quirinal Hill, built in 302 BCE. Salus was often depicted in art with snakes and a bowl. Her festival was celebrated annually on March 30th. The name Salus is Latin for health and is the root of English words such as salubrity and salutation.
